study.title: Job 22 - Elifaz accuses, advises and promises restoration
study.overview: In this chapter, Eliphaz makes the third and final major intervention of the discourse cycle. He begins by denying that Job's righteousness can bring some benefit to God and from there, accuses Job of concrete sins of social injustice and practical irreverence. He then compares the fate of the ancient wicked with Job's current situation, suggesting that his suffering is a sign of guilt. Finally, he calls Job to repentance, promising that if he turns to the Almighty, he will find peace, prayer answered and material restoration. The chapter is important because it shows how true advice on repentance can be mixed with unjust accusations and wrongly applied to an innocent person.

outline.title: The accusation that God wins nothing with Job's righteousness
outline.explanation: Eliphaz questions whether human righteousness can benefit God or enrich the Almighty. This line prepares his suspicion that Job, in defending himself, would be insinuating that God treats him with injustice. The biblical text, however, does not show Job by affirming this in a direct way, but by lamenting his suffering.

outline.title: The denunciation of injustice and comparison with the ancient wicked
outline.explanation: Eliphaz attributes to Job exploitation of the weak, hardness with the poor, widows and orphans, and then says that the wicked of the past were overthrown by God. He uses examples of ancient judgment to reinforce the idea that the calamity present proves guilt. The notes highlight that he treats this as if it were direct application to Job's situation, although reasoning is debatable.

outline.title: The Call to Repentance and the Promise of Restoration
outline.explanation: Eliphaz calls on Job to be reconciled to God, to accept divine instruction, and to turn away wickedness. He promises that God will be his treasure, will answer his prayer and make his life enlightened. The end of the chapter expresses the conviction that the prayer of the righteous can benefit even others, but also contains a promise of prosperity that the notes present as an unduly applied principle to Job.

study.context: According to the notes, this excerpt belongs to the third round of speeches between Job and his friends. Eliphaz speaks after Job's answers and before new replicas. He interprets Job's suffering as evidence of sin, while the book as a whole had already presented Job as intact. The notes also note that Eliphaz uses examples of God's judgment on the wicked ancients to support his argumentation.
study.theology: The chapter confronts the relationship between human justice and the character of God. In correct terms, righteousness adds nothing to God, but manifests his glory; therefore, Eliphaz's question in 22:2-3 touches a real truth, though it used in an accusatory manner. The text also teaches that God sees everything and judges in a holy way, rejecting the idea that darkness prevents him from acting. At the same time, the chapter shows the danger of turning true doctrines into automatic accusations against a sufferer: Eliphaz speaks correctly about repentance, prayer, and peace with God, but errs in assuming that Job's affliction proves specific crimes. The promise that God will hear, restore, and will be treasure for the believer points to God's sufficiency, but should not be read as a mechanical formula of prosperity.

scholarViews.insight: Eliphaz did not understand that God is pleased with the righteousness of the righteous, and yet the accusation he makes to Job is applied wrongly; Job's righteousness should rather exalt the glory of God.
Eliphaz's question is true in itself, but it was unjustly applied to Job; he mixes a correct doctrine with an undue accusation.
Eliphaz exposes the greatness and justice of God, but then promises Job great wealth and prosperity if he repents.

questions: When we use correct biblical truths, are we also applying them with justice and discernment to others?
How does the chapter teach that suffering should not be automatically treated as proof of specific guilt?
How can we distinguish a legitimate call to repentance from a precipitated accusation against someone who suffers?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine his own heart before explaining the suffering of others. It is wise to confess sins when they exist, seek reconciliation with God and value their instruction, but without turning distress into a sentence against the other. In practice, we must unite truth and meekness: to speak of repentance with seriousness, to pray for those who suffer and to avoid hard conclusions based only on circumstances. We are also reminded that the greatest good is not prosperity, but God himself as treasure, peace and response to prayer.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not clarify whether the last sentence of verse 30 should be understood exactly as the salvation of third parties because of the purity of one's hands, or as the release of the innocent by the righteousness of that righteous. There is also implicit divergence between commentators on how best to translate and apply this line. In addition, the chapter contains Elifaz's assertions that are interpretative and should not be taken as a direct and infallible statement about Job's case.
